items.abstract: <jats:p>Enterprise API integration remains a costly and time-consuming process due to manual sandbox creation, inconsistent documentation, and delayed partner onboarding. This paper presents an AI-governed Core Virtual API Engine that converts API specifications into autonomous sandbox environments using template-driven virtualization, governance validation, synthetic data generation, and automated deployment. The proposed framework accepts multiple API contract formats, converts them into OpenAPI specifications, validates them against OpenAPI standards and enterprise governance templates, generates database and endpoint templates, creates synthetic test data, produces Postman collections, deploys sandbox environments, and performs automatic cleanup of idle resources. This approach reduces manual sandbox setup effort, improves developer onboarding, and enables scalable enterprise API virtualization.</jats:p>
title: Autonomous API Sandbox Generation Using Agentic AI

items.abstract:
<jats:p><p>Background. Human-AI interaction has moved from a human-computer interaction research topic to an operational and regulatory concern. The April 2025 rollback of an OpenAI model update after the system became, in the company's own characterisation, overly flattering or agreeable, the March 2026 Science publication demonstrating that sycophantic AI reduces prosocial intentions and promotes dependence, and the August 2026 implementation deadline for European Union AI Act Article 14 human oversight requirements have placed appropriate reliance, calibrated trust, and meaningful oversight at the centre of practitioner and regulatory attention. The literature, however, remains fragmented across disciplines, modalities, and jurisdictions.</p>
<p>Purpose. This paper provides a comprehensive synthesis of human-AI interaction research and practice across three contemporary AI modalities, predictive, generative, and agentic, and integrates this synthesis with the regulatory architectures emerging in the European Union and the Gulf Cooperation Council. The paper is designed as a reference contribution for the wider fifteen-paper slate and as a scholar-practitioner resource for senior cybersecurity, governance, and risk audiences.</p>
<p>Approach. The paper adopts a narrative review methodology combining contemporary 2024 to 2026 empirical literature on trust calibration, appropriate reliance, and oversight effectiveness; primary regulatory document analysis (the EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI Risk Management Framework, UAE Information Assurance Standards, UAE Personal Data Protection Law, the UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, and Saudi Arabian regulatory instruments); and analysis of recent documented incidents including the OpenAI sycophancy rollback and the body of academic work on emergent sycophancy in large language models.</p>
<p>Findings. Three observations emerge from the synthesis. First, the constructs of trust, calibration, and reliance, while conceptually distinct, are increasingly conflated in practitioner discourse; appropriate reliance, the behavioural outcome that practitioner and regulatory frameworks ultimately require, is empirically distinguishable from trust as an attitude and warrants separate measurement. Second, the modality-specific risk profiles differ substantially: predictive AI risks are concentrated in confidence miscalibration and rubber-stamp oversight; generative AI risks are concentrated in sycophancy and anthropomorphic trust manipulation; agentic AI risks are concentrated in oversight tractability as system autonomy increases. Third, the EU AI Act Article 14 oversight architecture is more developed than its GCC counterparts, but GCC regulatory instruments include user awareness, transparency, and cultural appropriateness considerations that EU instruments under-address; cultural bias documented in large language models toward Western entities creates a trust calibration problem in Arabic-speaking user populations that has a limited counterpart in EU deployment contexts.</p>
<p>Implications. Practitioners deploying AI systems across modalities should distinguish trust, calibration, and reliance in their human factors design and assessment. Multi-jurisdictional deployments in the GCC require interaction design that accommodates both EU AI Act oversight obligations and GCC-specific cultural, linguistic, and regulatory expectations. Empirical validation through practitioner vignette surveys is reserved for subsequent research in this slate. Future work will extend the analysis through comparative regulatory mapping (Paper 14) and the assessment of dual-use interaction risks (Paper 12).</p></jats:p>
title: Human-AI Interaction Across Predictive, Generative, and Agentic AI

items.abstract: <jats:p>Multitasking is indispensable in modern service operations, forcing human employees to divide their limited cognitive capacity across concurrent interactions. While traditional literature views humans as isolated executors who adapt their coping behavior under pressure, the integration of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) fundamentally reshapes this paradigm. In hybrid service systems, human employees retain the operational discretion to dynamically delegate tasks to the agentic AI. However, because effective delegation requires significant cognitive effort, a fundamental tension emerge. The intense workload that drives employees to rely on AI simultaneously degrades their ability to delegate tasks optimally. Thus, it is uncertain whether agentic algorithms mitigate the traditional costs of multitasking or introduce new unintended behavioral failures. We take the first step to empirically investigate how multitasking pressure affects service outcomes in these hybrid settings, and to what extent delegation quality mediates this relationship. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset from a leading smart home company and employing an instrument variable approach, we document that multitasking increases overall sales by 8.17% but severely degrades customer emotion by 0.8 percentage points at the session level. Opening the black box of hybrid collaboration, we reveal that operational pressure acts as a catalyst for both effective task offloading and ineffective workload dumping. For transactional outcomes (sales), the massive informational efficiency generated by effective AI delegation easily offsets occasional human errors, creating a net-positive technological buffer. Conversely, for relational outcomes (customer emotion), while the effective AI delegation successfully buffers the informational demands, the customer's emotional experience still collapses. We resolve this puzzle by decoupling algorithmic failure from human cognitive depletion. We demonstrate that under multitasking pressure, human employees systematically curtail conversational efforts to survive the workload. Specifically, they reduce affective sentiment score by 0.38 percentage points and message length by 0.49% at the session level. This suggests that in hybrid operations, the true structural bottleneck is not algorithmic limitation, but the unavoidable affective and communicative withdrawal of the overloaded human employee. Our findings offer profound implications for service managers to implement dynamic concurrency routing, decouple technical execution from relational repair, and restructure employee performance appraisals, to safeguard customer experience.</jats:p>
title: When Human Multitasking Meets Agentic AI in Hybrid Service Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>As agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems take on more autonomous roles within complex sociotechnical settings, the way human operators cognitively interact with automation is fundamentally changing. This systematic review compiles evidence from 120 empirical and conceptual studies published between 2012 and 2026 to investigate the human‑factor dimensions—skill erosion, cognitive dependency, automation bias, trust calibration, situation awareness, human supervision, and human‑AI collaboration—that influence whether hybrid human‑agentic AI systems stay trustworthy, resilient, and cognitively sustainable. Using PRISMA 2020 guidelines, studies were retrieved from multiple databases programmatically, screened for language, abstract completeness, DOI validity, and publication year, and evaluated for relevance with a weighted keyword scoring system. Findings show a rapidly increasing publication rate (68 studies appeared in 2026 alone), with healthcare and engineering leading the fields; the most common research themes were deskilling (n = 42), cognitive dependency (n = 30), and trust calibration (n = 20). The synthesis highlights key tensions between the efficiency gains offered by AI and the gradual loss of human expertise, and introduces the Cognitive Sustainability and Trust Calibration (CSTC) Framework as a new integrative model for designing and governing hybrid AI systems. Practical implications include reforms in clinical education, governance of agentic AI, and interface standards to support appropriate reliance. Quality appraisal with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) revealed that most included studies achieved moderate to low risk, while Egger&apos;s test indicated significant funnel-plot asymmetry (p < 0.001). This review offers a solid empirical basis for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers at the cutting edge of trustworthy human‑AI integration.</jats:p>
title: Human Factors and Cognitive Sustainability in Trustworthy Hybrid Human–Agentic AI Systems: A Systematic Review
